“In all hard work there is profit, but the talk of the lips leads only to poverty” (Proverbs 14:23).

This sentence is the starting point of this entire module. Notice what it does not say. It does not say: all prestigious work. It does not say: all well-paid work either. It says: all hard work. God put abundance in work, not in speeches, nor in dreams that are never put into action.

1. Work, the entry door

Before receiving anything else, man received a job: God “put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Work is therefore not a punishment. The weariness and the sweat came later (Genesis 3:17-19), but work itself was there from the start. Whoever works honestly honors God and opens a door. “He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth” (Proverbs 10:4).

2. You can start from anywhere

Ask the question around you: who can become rich? Many will answer: the one who has had a lot of schooling, the one who has a big position, the one whose father has money. That is incomplete, and often false. Wealth does not start at one particular place. It starts where you are, with what you have.

You can start as a garbage collector. You can start as a janitor, a guard, a housekeeper, a laborer, a market seller, an apprentice, a driver. You can also start with a job of great value: manager, engineer, teacher, doctor. The starting point is not the same, but the road is the same: work faithfully, learn, become more valuable, set aside, then make what you have set aside bear fruit, and keep moving forward. The janitor who saves and trains himself can surpass the manager who spends everything he earns. And the reverse is also true: a big salary saves no one who does not know how to keep.

The Bible is full of humble beginnings. Ruth, a foreigner and a widow, starts by gleaning behind the reapers (Ruth 2). She will become the great-grandmother of King David. Joseph goes from slavery to prison, then becomes the second most powerful man in Egypt (Genesis 39-41). God invites his people not to despise the day of small things (Zechariah 4:10). What matters is not the size of the start, but faithfulness with what you have in your hands: “You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew 25:21).

Perhaps you don’t even have a job yet. You are searching, and every week that passes weighs a little heavier. This module is also for you: we will see how to find a job, how to keep it, and then how to move up in it.

3. How far can the road lead? Financial freedom

What do we call financial freedom? It is not becoming a billionaire, nor never working again. It is reaching the day when your essential needs are covered without you being at the mercy of a single boss, a single salary, or a single creditor. You have savings for the bad days. You have no debts choking you. Your income does not come from a single source. And you can choose what you do with your days.

This freedom is not an end in itself. Remember what we said in the first key: succeeding is not only getting rich. Financial freedom gives you the means to serve more widely: take care of your family, build a business that gives others a living, support the work of God, help those at the bottom.

You don’t get there in a day. You get there step by step: a job, an income, savings, one more skill, one more activity, an investment. “Wealth gained dishonestly dwindles away, but he who gathers by hand makes it grow” (Proverbs 13:11). By hand, little by little: that is God’s pace, and it is also the pace that lasts.

4. What you will find in this module

This module follows the path of an economic life, from the first step to building. Here is what it contains.

The partWhat you will learn
Preliminary: the 8 keys to successSee success the way God sees it, remove the blocks in your head, draw yourself a map, get trained, seize opportunities.
LeadershipKnow how to lead, first yourself, then others: vision, integrity, loyalty, handling conflicts.
Project managementTurn an idea into a result: the five phases, simple tools, mistakes to avoid.
Entrepreneurship essentialsFind a good idea, study the market, build a business model and a business plan, find funding, legally create your business.
Securing a jobLook for a job or learn a trade, without paying or lying, avoid scams, read your contract, get through your first 90 days.
Advancing in your jobBecome more valuable, talk about money with your employer, know your contract, move forward.
Career change without breaking the chainMove from one path to another without losing everything: the bridge, the test, the training.
Managing your businessSeparate the money, keep your accounts, calculate your price, invoice, get paid.
InvestingUnderstand before putting your money in, and recognize scams.
Rebuilding after bankruptcyFor those who have fallen from a height: take stock, count what is left, decide where to go, and make a plan.

5. Three things to remember before you begin

Honest work is the only solid road. Shortcuts, bribes, and scams promise abundance and deliver poverty. What is acquired dishonestly does not last.

Start where you are. Not where you would like to be, nor where others were. With what you have, today, take a step in the right direction.

You can fall and get back up. You will see at the end of this module that the Bible does not hide falls. Even someone who has lost everything can rebuild, if they accept to count what is left and start again from there.

All work produces abundance. Start where you are, with what you have, and move forward little by little.

1. Make the difference

“There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy on men: a man to whom God gives riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing for his soul of all that he desires, yet God gives him no power to eat of it, but an alien eats it. This is vanity, and it is an evil disease. If a man fathers a hundred children, and lives many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul is not filled with good, and moreover he has no burial; I say, that a stillborn child is better than he: for it comes in vanity, and departs in darkness, and its name is covered with darkness. Moreover it has not seen the sun nor known it. This has rest rather than the other. Yes, though he live a thousand years twice told, and yet fails to enjoy good, don’t all go to one place? All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.” (Ecclesiastes 6:1-7)

Many of us tend to think that succeeding in life means getting rich. This is certainly not the case. Wealth can be the fruit of a successful life, but it is not success itself. The inability to grasp this idea is why most people fail in life before they have even started.

Succeeding in life means, above all, finding meaning in it. Why am I here? What am I for? What will be the outcome? What is in it for me? What benefit for those around me? In general, we are in this world to live. Yes, God created us so that we would live. We are not here to survive but to live.

Succeeding means, above all, managing to live. By living, we give pleasure to the givers of life. Have you ever seen a person wear with pride and joy a garment you gave them? How did you feel? Very happy, didn’t you? It is a little like the feeling that moves God when he sees us truly living. If you have difficulty with the expression “glorify God,” we can say the problem is settled now. You are here to live, and in doing so you will give pleasure to God, who created you for this. That is what “glorifying God” means.

When you live, you no longer fight. It becomes easier to share the world with those around us and with the other components of nature. Indeed, you no longer force yourself to be in harmony with your environment. On the contrary, this harmony becomes natural and you become useful and beneficial to those around you, and vice versa. Succeeding in life means living without regret. It means using your mental and physical faculties to innovate, create, organize, lead, and govern along a line that you have drawn for yourself with a clear conscience.

When we do this, we may make mistakes and suffer setbacks, but we have no regret. On the contrary, in the end we achieve accomplishments that make ourselves and the whole world smile.

2. Remove the perilous block

The main block to success in life and in its different areas is a wrong attitude toward finances. Most human beings focus on money. They let themselves be blocked by money. They generally think like this: “When I have a little money, I will do this and that…” They have ideas, but before they even begin to think them through, they think of the money that is not there. From that moment, they stop, drop the project, and go back to the everyday routine.

The day they come across a sum of money that could help put that idea in place, they will do nothing. They will spend it on the routine and wait again for that means that will never come.

When they do happen to start something, they concentrate on the return on investment, so that discouragement can keep them from persevering.

You must overcome this mistake. You will probably never have in hand all the money needed to start something. You may have to do a number of things without a penny. Most of them will be described in this book. It is by doing them that you will position yourself, despite your financial situation, at the level you desire.

3. Succeed in your head

A man is the product of his thoughts. If you think you are nothing, you are nothing. And if that is the case, no one in the whole world, God included, will be able to help you. If you think yourself incapable, you really are incapable!

It is possible that you currently have no great financial means, no training, no diploma, and none of the knowledge required to reach the goal that is the vision of your heart. But that does not mean you cannot reach it. On the contrary, you can do everything you desire. You can get there, you can reach it, you can be what you want.

This is not to say what is usually said: “you are destined for this.” No! No one is destined for anything at the expense of someone else. We certainly have different abilities, but we are all destined for greatness. It is to the human race that God gave this command: “Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth” (Genesis 1:28). So you can reach the goal you have. Think that you can!

However, you must know that you are in the world. You are not yet in paradise. It is in paradise that everything runs like clockwork. Here on earth, there are ups and downs. So you must expect the best and prepare for the worst. Everyone who has reached the summit of professional and financial achievement has known great setbacks. So you must expect to know failures, disappointments, and so on. You must prepare to be deceived and betrayed. Expect to be rejected, slandered, and insulted. And it is by braving all these obstacles that you will reach your goals and obtain the gain. You may know this passage of the Bible: “No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). The expression “all these things” stands for the setbacks suffered on the road to success. But the outcome is clear: WE ARE MORE THAN CONQUERORS.

So use what you have: your head! The Bible says, “He who heeds the Word finds prosperity. Whoever trusts in Yahweh is blessed” (Proverbs 16:20). You must use your head. Start by trying to find out what you are passionate about, then discover your world. And finally, look into how you can sell what you have.

4. Draw yourself a map

You need to be precise, concise, and focused. We live in a world that distracts. The world does not only use distractions to pull our attention away from what matters. It uses our needs, our loved ones, and our appetites… And that is where the trap is bigger. When you look at the urgent need of the moment, it becomes a great battle to concentrate on something in the future. That is why you need to know what you want to achieve. Then you must put it in plain view so you can stay focused.

  1. So write down what you are passionate about. This is called a dream.
  2. Decide what you will do with it and write that down too. This is called a vision.
  3. Deduce from it the work it requires of you. That is your mission.
  4. Write down all the details, the needs, the resource people, the inventions, and so on. Looking closely, you will see your goals.
  5. Arrange the above and set deadlines. You will have a plan.
  6. Based on all this, decide on the adjustments to make in your habits. You have values.

If you respect your values, even if everything does not go according to your plans, you will still find the means to reach your goals and fulfill your vision. That is how you succeed in life.

5. Get trained

To be a sailor, you must know how to swim. In every sailor recruitment exam, there will always be swimming tests. If a person has all the academic qualifications but cannot swim, they must take swimming lessons very early. They must take their lessons long before the exam period. If they wait for the exam announcement to take those swimming lessons, they will not succeed in becoming what they desire. They don’t need to take paid lessons. They simply have to know how to swim. It is possible to be excellent at swimming without taking paid swimming lessons.

The same goes for everything in life. To do anything, you need certain skills. You have to learn them. You don’t need to take paid training, unless you need diplomas to prove those skills. But even there, you can put things in perspective. And if you already have these abilities, keep developing them every day.

6. Seize opportunities

Those who are ready find opportunities. Those who are not prepared never find any. Make sure you are ready. If you have not met the opportunity so far, it is probably because you are not yet ready. So the essential thing about opportunities is that, in general, the one who creates them is also the one who seizes them.

You are already creating opportunities for yourself when you get trained and develop your skills. Indeed, you will be able to apply for positions when you hear about them. Likewise, you will be able to take part in competitive exams when they are launched… It is not on the day you hear about some opportunity that you seize it. It is long before, by preparing through training and daily practice.

There is something even better in creating and seizing opportunities. You can turn into a business what you know how to do, and for which you are often asked for free. A little advertising, a little marketing strategy, and you have a business. You don’t need a physical office. If you need space, you can start by rearranging your living room.

Your environment, your world, needs you. It wants to pay for your services. It only needs to know that you are there. So it is up to you to find out and to know your surroundings thoroughly. What do you know about your part of town? The residents? The businesses? The eating habits, the clothing habits…? Observe carefully and you will see! If the opportunity is not on the right side, it will be on the wrong side.

It was in 8th grade that one of my teachers told us this story, which has stayed with me ever since: two companies involved in shoe manufacturing send agents to a somewhat remote area to explore the market. Upon arrival, the observation was the same. None of the residents wears shoes. They were even looked at strangely by the residents because they had shoes on their feet. The first one takes his phone and calls his director: “Market with no potential, people don’t wear shoes.” The second also makes his call: “Market with great potential, people don’t wear shoes.” And you, what do you say? Your success will depend on it.

7. Write down projects

If someone gave you five million CFA francs right now, what would you do with it? If you hesitate for even a moment, you are your own problem. You are the block in your life. You are the enemy you have been praying against all along. And bad news: angels will not be able to remove this block! You must not look for money to eat. You must look for finances to put to good use. If everyone spent their time consuming, the earth would have disappeared along with its inhabitants.

The question then arises: what do you want to accomplish? In what field? What percentage will the return on investment be relative to the capital? How many jobs will it create? What new product? What usefulness? What progress for the neighborhood, the city, or the nation?

Don’t tell yourself: “If I find such and such a sum, I will do such and such a thing with it.” That is not true. Think first of an activity, an invention, a transformation, a product… Think about the components. Determine the gain generated in 1 year, over 5 years and more. Think about the equipment and staff needed at the start. Make objective plans. Don’t take into account what you have. Take into account what you want and what is needed. Write it all down. That is what is called a project. You have already written it. Shape it and keep it within reach and in mind. You can have all the capital together. You can also set things up drop by drop according to the financial openings available. What matters is putting the project in place. And God forbids despising small beginnings.

8. Walking on quicksand

We said that life is made of ups and downs. So much so that investing yourself in anything is called a “risk.” Even if you don’t yet have money to put into something, you have time, physical energy, and so on. And if you do all this, put your heart into it, and the result turns out to be a fiasco? You will start again! Won’t you? You will start again and again, with a new strategy, study, attention… And if you do that until you end up in the grave? Did you say: “God forbid”? I answer: AMEN!

Indeed, God wants to help you succeed. If you ask him, he will. Don’t be mistaken. Far be it from me to ask you to become a church acolyte. But I want to tell you that you can try to succeed until you die if you leave God aside!

You surely know the stories of people who have made great achievements and reached magnificent breakthroughs in finance, technology, politics, and other fields without making faith in God a concern. Many of these people seem to have lived happily. I am not saying that they were not or that they are not. I am saying rather that they appear happy. So you too can, it seems, succeed in your life and enjoy happiness without worrying about God.

However, doubts remain. You can achieve great things in your life and for those around you. That is a success that has nothing to do with what you really want. Because at the end of all this, you may have only regrets, regrets greater and more numerous than joys. Let us nevertheless repeat with emphasis that you can accomplish great things that benefit many people in the world, make fortunes for yourself and gain prestige without concerning yourself with faith in Christ. Apply the rules well and you can find the right answers and succeed. Moreover, if you pray to God with all your strength without applying the rules, you will get nowhere.

Yet you know as well as I do that forces in the shadows may try to hold you back. In fact, these forces can manage to stop you or pull you down! It is against this that you must find a solution. God is the only one able to put them all out of action. And you can count on him, if you accept his salvation in Jesus Christ.

lecons.titre: Leadership: what keeps a leader standing
lecons.html:
What is a leader?

Ask the question around you: “What is a leader?” Many will answer with a title. The director. The pastor. The president of the association, the one who signs at the bottom of the page. We confuse leadership with the position one holds. Yet you all know a boss who leads no one, and someone with no title at all whom everyone listens to.

Leadership is the influence you have on others, and what you do with it. Whoever puts it at the service of those he leads, to guide them and help them grow, is a leader. Whoever uses it to dominate is not one, even with the finest office in town. Jesus said it plainly: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.” (Matthew 20:26) Notice that he does not ask his disciples to give up wanting to be great. He shows them the way to get there.

A. What keeps a leader standing

1. Knowing where you are going

A leader who does not know where he is going will still arrive somewhere, with everyone behind him. Vision is the heading. It does not need to be grandiose, but it must be clear enough to be said in two sentences to someone who is tired. “Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint; but one who keeps the law is blessed.” (Proverbs 29:18) Take the test: ask your youngest co-worker where you are going. If he hesitates, the problem is not with him.

2. Being the same in public and in private

That is integrity. Imagine a treasurer who talks about honesty on Sunday and helps himself from the cash box on Monday. Everyone ends up knowing, and none of his speeches goes through anymore. Trust is built over years and lost in one afternoon. Without agreement between what we say and what we do, everything else is just decoration.

3. Standing firm when it is not popular

Having courage does not mean not being afraid. It means deciding in spite of fear. Announcing bad news to the team. Refusing a dishonest shortcut that would pay off big. Staying on your feet when the criticism comes and friends become scarce. The true leader does what is right, even if no one applauds. Especially if no one applauds.

4. Respecting, even in disagreement

In front of you is a person, with their dignity. You can say no to an idea without despising the one who carries it. When you respect someone you disagree with, you get their cooperation. When you despise them, you get a conflict, even if you won the discussion.

5. Mastering yourself

The leader who explodes at every frustration teaches his team to hide problems. No one dares tell him the truth anymore, and one day it arrives on its own, bigger. Keeping control of your words, your reactions, and your emotions is not a matter of natural character. It is daily work.

lecons.titre: Loyalty, conflicts, and three leaders of the Bible
lecons.html:
B. Loyalty, the backbone of leadership

Loyalty means staying faithful to a vision, a mission, or a team. Careful: it is not blind submission. You can be loyal and tell your boss he is wrong. Being loyal means keeping your commitments with integrity, including when the storm comes and leaving would be easier.

Concretely, a loyal leader keeps his convictions from one day to the next and does not change his message depending on the person in front of him. He protects his co-workers: he defends them before his superiors and corrects them only in private. He takes responsibility. And he stays just, even when justice costs him something. “A faithful man is rich with blessings.” (Proverbs 28:20)

The Bible gives us a striking example: Jonathan. He is the son of King Saul, the heir to the throne. He understands that David is the one God has chosen. He could have seen a rival in him. He chooses to be his friend and to support him, even to the point of telling him: “You will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you.” (1 Samuel 23:17) He put truth before power, at the cost of his own place.

C. Conflicts: build rather than break

Leadership is not seen only in victories. It is seen in how we handle tensions. A good leader does not try to avoid conflicts. He faces them with maturity and with justice.

Let’s take a situation you have probably already known. Two team members are each convinced that the other took the credit for shared work, and each has come to talk to you about it in private. What do you do? Here is what works. First, truly listen to each one, without preparing your answer while they speak. Then, separate the problem from the person, because you can solve a problem without destroying someone. Seek the truth without breaking the peace, which takes patience. And correct with kindness, so that the other person can improve and does not merely feel judged.

The goal is peace: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.” (Matthew 5:9) Look at the word: makers. Peace does not fall from heaven, it is made.

Nehemiah is a good example. While he was rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, he faced everything: the mockery of enemies, the injustices of the rich against the poor of his own people, the divisions. He gathered the people, corrected what needed to be corrected, and kept building. When they tried to pull him away from his building site, he answered: “I am doing a great work, so that I can’t come down.” (Nehemiah 6:3)

D. Three leaders of the Bible

Moses

Moses did not look for the position. When God calls him, he answers that he is not an easy speaker (Exodus 4:10) and tries to wriggle out. Yet he did not flee his mission. His strength came from his closeness to God: “Yahweh spoke to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.” (Exodus 33:11) Facing the people’s complaints, crises, and rebellions, he remained concerned for justice. And above all, he carried this people, even when they hardly deserved it, interceding for them again and again.

Jonathan

Jonathan, as we have seen, shows leadership of humility. The rightful heir, he accepts being second. A faithful friend and discreet strategist, he put his convictions and the mission God had entrusted to David above his own advancement.

Nehemiah

Nehemiah shows what a clear vision produces when it is carried with courage. He mobilizes, he plans, he builds despite opposition. He also knew how to reconcile his brothers when they were tearing each other apart, without ever losing sight of his mission.

lecons.titre: What destroys a leader, leadership and entrepreneurship
lecons.html:
E. What destroys a leader

A leader rarely fails for lack of skills. He most often fails because he loses his bearings. Four things are waiting for him around the corner: pride, manipulation, emotional instability, and the betrayal of his own values. They almost never come together. Pride opens the door, and the others walk in behind it.

Saul serves as our warning. On the day he is chosen king, he cannot be found: he has hidden himself among the baggage (1 Samuel 10:22). He is not arrogant. Then power arrives. Jealousy toward David sets in, disobedience follows, and finally he refuses to hear the truth. He had started with God’s anointing. He ended up losing his heart.

What to remember

Leadership is a gift, a responsibility, and a mission. It is not an ego game, nor an authority to impose. It is a path of service. If you must keep only three things: a vision you can state in two sentences, a loyalty that does not depend on the mood of the day, and calm when things heat up.

“Don’t try to be a boss, try to be a faithful servant. It is loyal servants who become true leaders.”

F. Leadership and entrepreneurship: the two cannot be separated

An entrepreneur is a leader in action. He does not just create a project: he must carry a vision, mobilize people, and face difficulties. All the qualities we have just seen are found, one by one, in the life of a business.

Leadership skillEntrepreneurial application
Clear visionSet a direction for the project, win over investors
IntegrityBuild a reliable reputation with partners
CourageMake risky decisions, own failure
RespectBuild loyalty among teams and customers
Self-masteryManage stress, delays, conflicts
LoyaltyStay faithful to the original mission despite obstacles
Conflict managementKeep the team united in times of tension

A good entrepreneur does not just manage numbers. He gives meaning to what his team does.

When leadership is weak, the business pays for it. An authoritarian boss sees his team lose heart. Without vision, you navigate blindly. When the boss says one thing and does another, partners keep their distance. And a poorly handled conflict ends in demotivation, sometimes in a breakup. Many projects do not fall because of a bad business model, but because of a leader with no direction or no values.

Let’s take our biblical examples again with an entrepreneur’s eyes. Moses had to convince, rally, face crises, and hold on despite exhaustion. Nehemiah was a true project manager: he planned, negotiated, motivated his team, and settled conflicts. Jonathan is the model of the loyal partner, even when competition is fierce. Saul reminds us that a man who is talented at the start can ruin his project through his excesses.

An entrepreneur is not first of all a business creator. He is someone who carries a purpose, who serves a mission, and who leads people. Without leadership, entrepreneurship stays dry. With healthy leadership, a project can become a work that lasts.

A. What is a project?

A project is not simply a good idea. It is a set of activities organized over time to achieve a specific result. It has a beginning and an end, clear objectives, and limited resources: people, equipment, money. It seeks to bring about a change or a solution to a given problem.

A few examples: setting up a natural juice stand, organizing a literacy campaign in a neighborhood, launching a small community farm. In each case, you can say when it starts, when it ends, and what you want to have at the end. If you cannot say it, you have a wish, not yet a project.

B. The five phases of a project

Almost all projects, small or large, go through the same five stages. Those who skip one find it again later, with interest.

1. Initiation

Everything begins with a real need or an opportunity. Ask yourself three very simple questions: what problem do I want to solve? for whom? and what will the result look like? You must be able to describe this result in words others understand, words that make them want to follow. Without a well-defined problem, the best solution in the world will be of no use to anyone.

2. Planning

This is the stage people like least, and it is the one that saves the most projects. You start by setting SMART objectives, that is, specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, and time-bound. “Helping young people” is not an objective. “Training ten young girls in sewing in six months” is.

Then you write the action plan: what to do, when, how, with whom. You list what is needed, in people, equipment, and money. And you draw up an estimated budget, with a margin for the unexpected, because there will be some. The goal of all this is to see the difficulties before they fall on you.

3. Execution

Here, you move into action. You gather the resources, you launch the planned activities, you talk regularly with the team and with everyone the project concerns. And the unexpected arrives: the supplier who doesn’t deliver, the rain that blocks the site, the sick co-worker. This phase demands rigor, leadership, and the flexibility to change route without losing sight of the destination.

4. Monitoring and control

Once the project is launched, you don’t let go of the wheel. Track progress: the schedule, the budget, the results. Use simple tools, like a progress report or a dashboard, and quickly look at the gap between what was planned and what is actually happening. A small delay spotted today costs little. The same delay discovered in three months costs a lot. Good monitoring protects your time, your money, and your team’s motivation.

5. Closing and evaluation

Many people stop as soon as it works. Yet a project that is not properly closed ends up forgotten, even if it succeeded. At the end, evaluate the results: what was accomplished, and what lessons can be drawn? Write an honest final report. Share the results, with testimonials, photos, summaries. And ask yourself whether the project can continue, be redone elsewhere, or give birth to another one.

lecons.titre: Project management: tools, mistakes, and a case study
lecons.html:
C. Four simple tools

You don’t need complicated software to start. A notebook and a bit of discipline are enough, even for a small project.

The toolWhat it is for
The planning tableSaying who does what, when, and with what means.
The simplified budgetComparing what you planned to spend with what you actually spent.
The tracking sheetRecording the activities carried out, the obstacles met, and the solutions applied.
The final reportSummarizing the results obtained, the lessons learned, and ideas for what comes next.

D. The mistakes we see all the time

Launching a project without a clear vision. Underestimating deadlines and costs: it almost always takes more time and money than planned. Not talking to your team. Not following the stages and anticipating nothing about blockages. And then giving up too fast, out of discouragement, sometimes just before it starts to work. These mistakes are almost all avoidable, provided you know them.

E. What helps you succeed

Start small, but well structured. Involve the beneficiaries from the design of the project: those you want to help know their problem better than you do. Write everything down, the stages, the ideas, the contacts, and the expenses, because memory is a very poor accountant. Look for an impact that lasts rather than a result that fades with the event. And surround yourself with reliable, honest co-workers who have skills different from yours.

F. Case study: an ABBA community sewing workshop

ElementProject content
Problem identifiedYoung girls out of school, with no activity and no income
General objectiveIntegrate ten young girls through training and production
Key activitiesBuying machines, sewing training, producing items, selling
Estimated budget400,000 FCFA
Partners mobilizedAn experienced craftsman, the local Church, community contributors

Look at what is good about this project. A precise problem. An objective you can count. Concrete activities. A budget. Partners. You can write it on one page and explain it to someone in three minutes. That is what you expect from a well-prepared project.

G. What the Bible says about it

The Bible has been talking about planning for a long time. Three verses are enough to lay the foundations.

“For which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn’t first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?” (Luke 14:28) Jesus does not say to start by praying and then see what happens. He asks us to sit down and count.

“Commit your deeds to Yahweh, and your plans shall succeed.” (Proverbs 16:3) You prepare your plan, and you hand it over to God. The two go together.

“Write the vision, and make it plain on tablets, that he who runs may read it.” (Habakkuk 2:2) What is not written stays in the head, and what stays in the head gets lost.

God loves clear vision, work well done, and the excellence that comes from faith.

H. Entrepreneurship and project management: the two hold together

Entrepreneurship is the realm of ideas. Project management is the method for turning them into reality. Why can’t the two be separated?

First, because every business venture is… a project. Opening a shop, creating a service, starting a farm, developing a platform: all of it goes through the stages we have just seen. Second, an entrepreneur who does not know how to plan is in danger. He risks misjudging his costs, seeing nothing coming, acting without an objective, and collapsing at the first unexpected event.

Project management also provides structure. It lets you go further than intuition or the energy of the moment, with benchmarks: a budget, deadlines, indicators, reviews. This is what allows a business not only to “start with passion,” but to last, grow, and be handed on.

Take a sister who wants to sell doughnuts. She asks herself: where do I buy the flour? how much do I invest? how many doughnuts must I sell to cover my costs? when will I be able to hire someone? Without knowing it, she is already doing project management. Entrepreneurship and project management meet from the very first questions.

In summary: entrepreneurship is the dream of creating something new and useful. Project management is the path that makes this dream possible, measurable, and lasting. A good entrepreneur is therefore, necessarily, a good project leader.

lecons.titre: Entrepreneurship: profile, idea, and the right person
lecons.html:
Choosing to start a business is not only wanting to be your own boss. The desire for independence attracts many people, but it is not enough. It takes strategy, endurance, faith (especially for the Christian entrepreneur), and solid skills. A good idea or a passion does not make a business. It also takes practical know-how, good reflexes, and the ability to lead. What follows gives you the essentials, in the order you will need them.

1. The entrepreneur’s profile

Successful entrepreneurs do not all look alike, but a few traits are found in them that anyone can work on. The first is a growth mindset: they take every failure as a lesson and keep training themselves all their lives. Then comes passion. It is not reduced to a preference: it is what makes you hold on when obstacles pile up, because it gives meaning to the effort.

They also know how to solve problems. Faced with an obstacle, they don’t stop: they look for how to get around it, defuse it, or make it a springboard. They take risks, but calculated risks. Starting a business means accepting uncertainty, not recklessness. They are resilient, that is, able to bounce back without giving up, to stay clear-headed when everything goes wrong, and to keep faith in their mission.

One last trait, a more recent one: online presence. Today, a business that cannot be found on the Internet is almost invisible. A social media account, a simple website, a bit of content: it has become necessary to grow, even for a small activity.

2. Finding a good business idea

Before the business plan and before financing, you need a solid idea. Here are several places to look for one.

Start with yourself. What do you know how to do? What do you do with ease, without even thinking about it? Your talents can become a unique offer. Then listen to what others say about you: repeated compliments, or people who often ask you for the same service, are valuable clues. Also look around you with a critical eye. Are everyday products and services practical? Can they be improved? Many innovations were born from simple observation.

Look for frustrations. What complicates your life, or that of your loved ones? Every problem can hide a business opportunity. Ask the question around you: what would you need to buy that doesn’t exist yet? You can also draw inspiration from elsewhere: trade fairs, trends in other countries, specialized magazines. And if you want to reduce risk, take over an activity that already exists and works, or partner with an already proven model.

3. Are you the right person for this project?

A good idea is not enough. You also have to be the right person to carry it. First take stock: list the skills your sector cannot do without (sales, management, marketing…), spot the ones you lack, and fill them through training or by teaming up with someone. Experience counts too. Knowing the sector greatly increases your chances, and the ideal is to start a business in a field you have already worked in.

Then look at your profile. An entrepreneur needs organization, autonomy, the ability to delegate, self-confidence that stays measured, and the ability to decide fairly quickly. Also think about your personal constraints: your family, your physical endurance, your financial situation, the regulatory obligations of your sector. And if you are launching with others, agree from the start on your motivations and expectations. A shared vision avoids many divorces.

lecons.titre: Market study, business model, marketing, and business plan
lecons.html:
4. The market study

The market study is the project’s compass. Without it, you move forward blind. It answers several questions.

The market itself

What are the trends in your sector? What needs are not yet met? How big is the market: your neighborhood, your city, the country, the region?

Demand

Who are your customers? What are their profiles, their buying habits, their expectations, what holds them back? Where do they get their information, at the market, on WhatsApp, on the radio? You cannot sell to someone you don’t know.

Supply

Who is already there? What do your competitors sell, at what price, with what image? What gaps or weaknesses can you exploit?

Two tools to see clearly

The PESTEL method reviews what can affect you from the outside: political, economic, social, technological, environmental, and legal factors. It helps you see coming the risks you don’t control. The SWOT tool (in French, FFOM) takes stock of you: your strengths (for example a rare skill), your weaknesses (few connections), your opportunities (a rising trend), and the threats (the arrival of a big competitor).

5. Building your business model

The business model is the way your business creates value, delivers it to its customers, and draws revenue from it. Four questions help clarify it. What need does your offer meet? What target does it address? What value does it bring that others don’t? How do you make money?

There are several ways to make money with the same idea:

The modelHow it works
FreemiumYou offer a free service, and charge for the options (especially for apps).
SubscriptionThe customer pays a regular amount: a monthly plan, a gym.
Low costLow prices, services reduced to the minimum.
AffiliationYou earn a commission for bringing a customer to another seller, often online.
Direct or home sellingYou go to the customer rather than waiting for them to come.
Pay per useYou pay only when you use: a motorbike-taxi ride, a car wash, a daily rental.

Your model must be consistent with your market, your resources, and your vision.

6. The marketing and sales strategy

An offer, even an excellent one, does not sell itself. You need a strategy to make it known. First set clear objectives, using the SMART method we saw in the section on project management. For example: “Reach 500 customers in 6 months” or “Increase by 20% the number of visitors who become customers within three months.”

Then define your targets precisely. Imagine typical customers, with a detailed portrait: “A 35-year-old woman, a manager in Cotonou, looking for local, healthy products, sensitive to ethical values.” The better you know this person, the more your message speaks to her.

Choose your means of action: advertising (local or online), social media, selling in a shop or on a platform, public relations, referrals or partnerships. Then track your results with simple tables: how much each new customer costs, how many visitors buy, whether customers are satisfied. And readjust according to what you discover.

7. The business plan

The business plan is a pivotal document. It organizes your project, makes it readable for investors or a bank, and guides you when you move into action. Here are its essential contents.

It begins with the presentation of the project: the idea, what extra it brings, your ambition. It presents the founding team: each person’s skills and role. It shows the market analysis, which proves that your offer meets a real need. It describes the business model and the sales strategy. And it ends with the financial forecasts: budget, break-even point, cash flow plan (we explain these notions in Part VII, “Managing your business”).

Don’t forget the executive summary, two pages at most, placed at the beginning. It is often the first thing people read, and sometimes the only one. It must captivate and convince.

8. Financing

There is not just one source of money, but several, which combine. Also remember what we said in module 11 about credit: before borrowing, calculate the real cost.

Money that comes from you and your loved ones

Personal contribution is the foundation. It shows your commitment and seriousness, and every financer looks at it first. Love money is money lent by loved ones: it can also give banks confidence, but always write down what is agreed, to protect the relationship. A tontine or a savings group can help gather a first capital. And if you have partners, a partner’s current account lets them temporarily advance money to the business. These sums are repayable later, and are recorded as a liability of the business.

Money that comes from institutions

Aid and grants: the State, local authorities, and development agencies sometimes offer support. In Benin, you can inquire at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry, APIEx, and the SME Development Agency. Some schemes come with training or technical support.

A business loan, from a bank or a microfinance institution, is used to finance equipment, premises, or working capital. It is repaid in several installments, with interest, over a period that varies widely from one lender to another. Leasing lets you rent a vehicle or equipment with an option to buy at the end of the contract: useful when buying immediately costs too much. Factoring is for businesses already operating: you “sell” your unpaid invoices to a company that pays you right away, for a commission. It is uncommon, but it improves cash flow.

Money that comes from investors

Business angels are experienced investors who bring money, but also advice and a network. They mostly choose innovative projects at the start-up stage, and take a share of the company’s capital. Crowdfunding goes through online platforms: you can receive donations, loans, or investments from many people. It is also a good way to test the public’s interest in your project. A variant, crowdlending, lets you obtain loans from individuals. These avenues are still little developed here: if you use them, check the platform seriously and beware of promises that are too good to be true (see Part VIII, on scams).

9. Choosing a legal status

This choice is important: it influences taxes, your liability, the way of running the business, and the manager’s social protection. In Benin, company law is that of OHADA.

Alone or with others? If you are alone, you can create a sole proprietorship, or a company with a single partner (a SARL can have just one person). With others, you turn to a SARL, a SAS, or a public limited company (SA).

Your personal assets. In a limited liability company, you risk only the amount of your contributions. In a sole proprietorship, your personal belongings answer for your debts: if the business collapses, the house can be affected.

The constraints of your sector. Certain regulated professions (health, law, insurance) require a specific status.

Your way of operating. The SARL is framed by law, which suits small teams and family businesses well. The SAS leaves a great deal of freedom in the articles of association and in the way of governing.

Your pay and social protection. Do you want to pay yourself through a salary, dividends, or both? Social contributions and the manager’s coverage depend on the status: inquire with the CNSS and an advisor before choosing.

Taxes. Depending on the size of the activity, the business pays a tax on profit or, for small businesses, a synthetic professional tax (TPS), which applies below 50 million F CFA of annual turnover. Each regime has its advantages depending on your goals: get advice.

10. Formalities for starting up (example: Benin)

Three routes are possible, from the lightest to the most structured.

The “entreprenant” status is a light status, for small activities. The formalities are simple. It is often the right starting point.

Trader, natural person. You create a sole proprietorship. There are a few more formalities, and your liability is unlimited.

The company. It is more structured and suited to growth, but it requires more documents: the articles of association, registration with the RCCM, and tax registration (IFU).

The business formalization desks and the SME Development Agency can support you. Ask them for the list of documents, costs, and current timelines, because they change. We come back to these points in Part VII.

11. The first months of activity

This is a delicate but exciting phase. It demands rigor, adaptability, and a great deal of commitment.

You will first immerse yourself in the job of business owner: learning to manage the money coming in and going out, your obligations, your relations with suppliers, administrations, and customers. Your priority is to sell. That means going toward potential customers, following up with them, and building loyalty among the first ones. Your first customers are the most precious: they are the ones who will talk about you.

From the start, meet your tax and social obligations (taxes, CNSS, VAT if it applies to you), to avoid penalties. Plan your deadlines, tax, social, and banking, so as not to be caught by surprise. Track your numbers with simple indicators: cash, turnover, margin, stock, and do regular reviews.

Cultivate your network. Take part in events, build alliances, take care of your online presence and your image. Be vigilant about fraudulent letters or messages claiming to come from official bodies: if in doubt, contact the body yourself. And above all, don’t stay alone. Seek the support of an accountant, a banker, a mentor, a support network. An isolated entrepreneur goes slower and makes more mistakes.

lecons.titre: Securing a job: the market, the paths, and the trades
lecons.html:
A module on wealth creation cannot be content with talking about those who advance in their jobs, those who start a business, or those who invest. We must first talk about the one who does not yet have work, or whose work does not give him enough to live on. This part begins for him.

1. A job, but not necessarily an income

In Benin, almost everyone works in one way or another. Official unemployment is very low: 2.4% in 2021-2022 according to the World Bank. Yet in the same period, underemployment affected about 72% of the working population, and about nine workers out of ten (90%) were in the informal sector. That means you have an activity, but it does not earn enough, or not regularly, or without a contract and without protection.

When young people themselves are asked, the picture is even harsher. In the Afrobarometer survey conducted in January 2024 among 1,200 adults (results published in August 2026), 51% of young people aged 18 to 35 say they are unemployed and looking for work. This figure does not contradict the official rate: it does not measure the same thing. It reflects what people say about their own situation, and the question was about salaried work.

(These figures give an idea of the situation. They change from one survey to another. Sources: World Bank, Benin, country overview (2021-2022 data); Afrobarometer, Policy Paper No. 105, “Youth employment in Benin,” August 2026.)

Our goal is therefore not only to find a job. It is to find a reasonably regular income, with a minimum of security, and to keep it. We said it in the introduction: all hard work brings profit (Proverbs 14:23), but not idle talk. Complaining about the market gets nothing moving. What moves things forward is a precise approach, repeated every week.

2. Four paths

When we say “looking for a job,” we often think of a single door. There are four.

The pathWhat it isWhat it requiresThe trap
Private-sector employmentYou are an employee of a company, with a contractAn honest CV, useful skills, a good interviewJobs with no written contract or declaration
Civil service and State agenciesHiring is by competitive exam, call for applications, or published offersA complete file, patience, and following official channelsPaying someone “who knows someone”
Organized independent activityYou sell a skill (sewing, IT, accounting, carpentry, care) to clientsA mastered trade, clients, regularityStaying without a clear price, without follow-up, without paperwork
The businessYou create a structure and you hireEverything we saw in the part on entrepreneurshipLaunching without having tested your idea

These paths are not mutually exclusive. Many people move forward in stages: a salaried job, then an activity on the side, then later a business. What matters is to know where you are and where you want to go.

For the civil service, I will not give you a list of competitive exams here, because the rules, dates, and required documents change. Go regularly to the government’s official portal, which publishes job offers, and to the websites of ministries and agencies. Trust no intermediary.

3. What an employer is really looking for

An employer hires someone because he hopes that person will bring in more than they cost. He looks at three things. First reliability: will he be on time, will he tell the truth, will he finish what he starts? Then competence: does he know how to do what I need? Finally attitude: will he learn, will he get along with others?

The diploma often opens the door. But it is competence and character that make you stay in the house. Many offers ask for experience, which discourages beginners. The answer is not to give up. It is to manufacture experience: an internship, volunteering in an association or in your congregation, a small assignment for a neighbor or a shopkeeper. Proof that you have done something is worth more than the claim that you are capable of it.

Young people see these obstacles clearly. Asked by Afrobarometer, they cite first the lack of adequate training or preparation (29%), then the reluctance to take certain jobs (19%) and the lack of experience demanded by employers (17%). The second point deserves a pause: a modest first job is nothing to be ashamed of. As we saw in the introduction, you can start from anywhere. What matters is what you learn there and what you do with it.

4. Don’t forget the trades

When we talk about looking for a job, we quickly think of the office and the CV. Yet a large part of activity rests on trades learned with the hands: sewing, hairdressing, carpentry, masonry, welding, mechanics, electricity, plumbing, refrigeration and air conditioning, agriculture, food processing. These trades have a great quality: they give you a skill that sells everywhere, and one day you can work for yourself. God himself filled Bezalel with his Spirit, “in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship” (Exodus 31:3). And “one who works his land will have an abundance of food” (Proverbs 28:19).

You learn a trade in two ways. Either in a vocational training center. Or through apprenticeship: you join a master craftsman or a small business and learn by working. In that case, agree in advance, in writing if possible, on the duration, on what you will learn, on the conditions, and on the certificate or attestation you will be given at the end. An apprentice who spends years learning nothing and with no paperwork is an unpaid worker. Inquire with the ANPE and the training centers in your department about the schemes that exist and the recognized certificates.

lecons.titre: Securing a job: saying what you offer, the CV, and the network
lecons.html:
5. Knowing how to say what you offer

“I’m looking for a job” tells nobody anything. People don’t know how to help you. Compare with: “I’m an accountant, with three years of experience in a wholesale business. I know how to run a cash register, do bank reconciliations, and use a spreadsheet. I’m looking for a position in a distribution or processing company.” There, someone can think of you when they hear about a need.

A sentence to prepare: “I am (my trade or skill). I know how to (two or three concrete things). I am looking for (the type of position or client).”

6. An honest CV and a short letter

The CV, on one page

Your CV fits on one page, two at most if you have a lot of experience. It contains your contact details (a number where you can be reached, a simple and serious email address), what you know how to do, your experience with the results you achieved, your training, and two or three people who can speak about you. Have it read over by someone who knows how to read: a spelling mistake is already an impression.

And above all, do not lie. A fake diploma, an invented experience, a fudged date, everything ends up being found out, and dismissal follows when it happens. “Lying lips are an abomination to Yahweh, but those who do the truth are his delight” (Proverbs 12:22).

The letter

When you are asked for a cover letter, write five to eight lines. Say which position you are writing for, why this company, and what you bring. Address it to a person when you can.

A sentence to start with: “I would like to apply for the position of (position). I have (two years) of experience in (field), and I have (a specific result). I would be happy to meet you to talk about it.”

7. Your network

Many positions are filled by people who know someone. This is not about scheming: we more readily recommend a person we trust. Write down ten people who might hear about a need: former colleagues, neighbors, brothers and sisters from the congregation, shopkeepers, former classmates. Tell each of them, with your sentence from the previous lesson, what you are looking for. Simply ask: “If you hear of something, will you think of me?” And remember to return the favor.

Being recommended is one thing. Buying a place is another. We come back to it below.

lecons.titre: Securing a job: where to look, the rhythm, and the interview
lecons.html:
8. Where to look

The ANPE, the National Employment Agency, is a free public service. It has an office in each of the country’s twelve departments. You can register there, receive guidance, attend workshops on job-search techniques, and consult job offers. It also runs support programs for self-employment. For example, in 2026, it opened free short practical training courses for one hundred and fifty job seekers, as part of its Self-Employment Support Program. Programs, dates, and conditions change: go to the nearest office to find out what is open today.

Official offers: the government portal publishes job offers, mostly recruitment of managers and specialists, as well as notices from agencies and ministries. Companies: drop by or write to them, even without an announcement. Your congregation, your partner, your associations: people talk to each other there, they know each other, and that is where many needs are voiced before being published.

Searching online

Many offers and contacts now go through the phone: job offer websites, professional networks like LinkedIn, and WhatsApp or Facebook pages and groups devoted to employment. This is useful, provided you stay cautious. Create a serious profile, with a decent photo, your trade, your skills, and your results, as in your CV. Follow the official pages of companies, the ANPE, and ministries. And remember that an offer seen on WhatsApp is no truer than any other: verify it with the company itself.

Three rules of caution. Never send your ID or personal documents to someone you have not been able to identify. Never pay to apply. Beware of an offer that promises a lot, asks for no experience, and pushes you to reply quickly.

Recruitment firms and temp agencies

A recruitment firm or temp agency is a company that looks for people on behalf of other companies. A serious firm is paid by the company that is hiring, not by the candidate. If you are asked for money to register, to review your file, or to “place” you, that is a warning sign (see section 11). Before registering, check that the organization really exists: an address, an office, references. Temp work can be a good way in: you gain experience and get known. But demand a written contract for each assignment.

9. A rhythm, like a job

Looking for a job is a job. Set yourself a weekly rhythm and stick to it: for example five people contacted, three applications sent, and one approach to an organization (ANPE, company, association). Write everything in a notebook, so you don’t forget to follow up.

DateWho or whereWhat I sent or saidReplyPlanned follow-up
MondayCompany XCV and letterNot yetThursday, by phone call

A polite follow-up after a few days is not pushiness: it is seriousness. Many applications are lost simply because nobody followed up on them.

10. The interview

Find out about the company before you go: what it does, what it sells. Be on time, clean, calm. Answer briefly and truthfully. When asked “why should we choose you?”, answer with a result, not an adjective: “I reduced delivery delays by 20%” is worth more than “I am serious and motivated.” Never speak ill of a former employer, even if he deserves it.

Also prepare your questions: what the job involves day to day, what type of contract, what pay, what start date. Don’t talk about money first, but don’t dodge the question either: a serious employer expects it.

lecons.titre: Securing a job: never pay to be hired
lecons.html:
11. Paying to be hired: a firm no

This is the hardest moment of the search: when the months go by, the family is counting on you, and someone tells you: “Give me this much, and I’ll get you in.” It is not a shortcut. It is corruption, and the Bible is clear: “You shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds those who have sight and perverts the words of the righteous” (Exodus 23:8).

There is a practical reason for this refusal. Whoever gives in to get in ends up accepting what the system asks of him: a bribe here, a signature he shouldn’t put there, and later schemes to move up. You would have come in through the door of injustice, and you will have to keep going through it. That is not who we are as children of God. And honesty, even if it costs you a delay, leaves you free: no one can blackmail you.

What you refuse: money asked of you outside official channels to “place” you, to “push through” your file, to “guarantee” you the exam. What is normal: the official fees for a file or an exam, when they exist. They are announced in the official notice and are paid through the channel it indicates.

Some signs of a hiring scam: you are asked to pay to take a test or to have a file reviewed, by Mobile Money to a personal number; you are promised a “guaranteed” position; the offer comes from a personal address and not from the institution; you are pressured (“tomorrow is too late”); you are offered a job abroad, with visa, ticket, and housing “assured” in exchange for a sum paid in advance. Always verify with the institution itself.

A remark about going abroad. Many dream of leaving, and crooks take advantage: fake job offers in Europe, Canada, or the Gulf countries, fake contracts, fake visas. A serious employer does not ask the candidate to pay money to a private person to “guarantee” their visa or position. Before paying anything, verify the employer, the offer, and the procedures with the official services: the ANPE, the ministry in charge of employment, the embassy or consulate of the country concerned.

An example (invented story). Rodrigue has been looking for a job for seven months. A man from his neighborhood tells him that for 250,000 F, he can get him into a government office. Rodrigue hesitates: his wife is expecting a child. He talks to his partner, who reminds him of Exodus 23:8. He refuses. Four months later, after an internship obtained through a friend from the congregation, he lands a contract with a company. Later, the man from the neighborhood is arrested for taking the money of ten families. (The figures are only there to give an example.)

lecons.titre: Securing a job: before signing and the first three months
lecons.html:
12. Before signing

The offer in writing

When a proposal arrives, joy may make you accept everything. Breathe. Ask for the offer in writing: the position, the salary, the start date, the duration, the place, the hours. An offer that exists only by word of mouth can disappear without anyone being responsible.

The written contract

Demand a written contract. The Labor Code provides that certain contracts must be written, and what is written protects you as much as your employer. Read it calmly, at home, and if you have any doubt, have someone competent read it before you sign. You will find in the part on the Labor Code in module 12 what you need to know about the law. Here is what you look for in the contract.

What it must sayWhy
Your position and your tasksSo that other tasks are not gradually added to you
Your salary, in figures, and the payment dateSo that “we’ll see” does not become “we don’t pay”
The duration: open-ended, or until what dateTo know what you can count on
The trial period, if there is one: its lengthSo that it does not extend indefinitely
The hours, the leaveTo be able to organize your life
How the contract can be ended (notice period)To leave or be dismissed properly

A few simple rules. Never sign a paper with blanks. Sign nothing you have not understood. Keep a copy signed by both parties. If the employer refuses anything in writing, that is a warning.

The trial period

The trial period is a test in both directions: the employer observes you, but you observe him too. Is he fair? Does he pay on time? Are people respected? If you are told “we’ll see at the end of the month,” ask for it to be written down, with the duration.

Fixed-term, open-ended, internship

An open-ended contract has no end date: it is the normal form of a stable job. A fixed-term contract has an end date: it is not bad in itself, but watch out for contracts that follow one another endlessly, because the law limits the cases where they can be used. An internship is not a job: it is for learning. Before accepting one, ask in writing for its duration, whether there is an allowance, and what you will learn. An internship that says nothing about any of this risks being unpaid work.

Social security registration

Ask your employer whether you are registered with the National Social Security Fund (CNSS). It is what protects you in case of a work accident and prepares your retirement. An employer who registers no one leaves you alone the day something happens. Inquire at the CNSS about what you concretely receive.

13. The first three months

These three months decide how you are seen. Arrive on time. Ask what is expected of you, and ask in writing or by restating it. Learn the names and the way things are done in the house. Don’t say “that’s not my job.” Note what you accomplish, with figures: you will need it later. And keep your integrity from day one: don’t take part in any arrangement that embarrasses you, even a small one. “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10).

14. When things don’t go well

If you are not paid, or if the promised contract doesn’t come, first talk to your employer about it, in writing, calmly. Keep a copy. If nothing moves, the labor inspector can receive you and try to conciliate, and if needed, the labor court is there. You will find the way in module 12. An employee who knows his rights and stays correct is hard to push aside.

15. A job is not a substitute for security

A job can be lost: the company closes, the position is cut, the contract is not renewed. Your real security is not only your job. It is also in an emergency savings fund (module 11), a skill that sells elsewhere, and a network of people who know you. A job gets lost. A skill remains.

lecons.titre: When you have no job: holding on and the 90-day plan
lecons.html:
16. Holding on when you have no work

Not letting yourself be defined

Not having work is a trial, but it does not tell you what you are worth. Joseph was thrown into prison without deserving it. Yet “Yahweh was with Joseph,” and the keeper of the prison committed to him the care of all the prisoners (Genesis 39:21-23). In a place where he had no title, he worked with care. That is what, later, got him called before Pharaoh.

Two dangers

The first is immobility: you wait, you tell yourself luck will come, and the months go by. The second is shame: you hide your situation, you no longer dare to speak, and you deprive yourself of the people who could help. Tell your family, your partner, your pastor. No one will help you if they don’t know you are looking.

Not carrying this alone

“Two are better than one… for if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10). Ask your partner to check in with you every week: did you keep your rhythm? Whom did you contact? A word of encouragement does not replace an application, but it gives you the strength to send one more.

If sadness, anxiety, or discouragement become too heavy, or if you can no longer sleep or eat, also talk to a doctor or a counselor. It is not a lack of faith: it is taking care of yourself.

17. The 90-day plan

Give yourself three months, in three stages.

PeriodWhat I do
Days 1 to 30: get my affairs in orderA one-page CV ready and proofread. Registration with the ANPE. The list of ten people to inform, with my sentence. A clear idea of what I can sell as a service. My essential expenses noted. A serious online profile, if my field lends itself to it.
Days 31 to 60: search and learnThe weekly rhythm kept (contacts, applications, one approach). A short training course, free if possible, in the target field. Volunteering or an internship to manufacture experience. If I have no trade, I look at an apprenticeship or a short training course.
Days 61 to 90: take stockWhat worked, what didn’t, who replied to me. I widen the search, change the angle if needed, and look at whether an independent activity can supplement.

After 90 days, you start again with what you have learned. You have gained experience and new contacts, and you are no longer in the same place as on day one.

18. In the meantime: an activity and controlled spending

A waiting activity

While searching, you can earn a little money honestly: a small service, a sale, helping a shopkeeper, an odd job. This is not giving up your search. It is staying on your feet, learning, and showing that you are not sitting with your arms crossed. But careful: a waiting activity must not stop you from continuing to search. Note what it earns and what it teaches you. One day it may become the start of a business (see the part on entrepreneurship).

Controlling your spending

Without a regular income, the money has to last. List your essential expenses: rent, food, transport, health, schooling. Cut the rest, without shame. If you have an emergency savings fund (module 11), now is when it is used. If you don’t, don’t rush into borrowing, especially not from lenders who charge enormous interest: one more debt during a job search is one more rope around the neck. Talk to your family and your congregation before going into debt.

19. An example (invented story)

Sylvain is 27, has a degree in management, and has searched for eight months with no result. He decides to follow a plan. During the first month, he prepares a one-page CV, registers with the ANPE, and informs ten people that he is looking for a position in accounting or stock management. He also offers a shopkeeper in his neighborhood to keep his cash book, for a small fee.

During the second month, he sends three applications a week and takes a short course on spreadsheets. The shopkeeper talks about him to a supplier, who is looking for someone for two months. Sylvain does an internship there. In the third month, the supplier offers him a fixed-term contract, which he asks for in writing before starting. (The figures and details are only there to give an example.)

To sum up

In Benin, official unemployment is low, but underemployment and the informal sector are very widespread: having an activity is not enough, you need an income that holds up. Young people themselves say that lack of preparation, refusal of certain jobs, and lack of experience hold back their entry into work. There are four paths: private-sector employment, the civil service, organized independent activity, and the business. Don’t forget the trades, learned through training or apprenticeship. An employer looks for reliability, competence, and a good attitude; if you lack experience, manufacture some. To search: an honest one-page CV, a short letter, ten people informed, the ANPE and official offers, online searching with caution, a weekly rhythm noted in a notebook, an interview prepared with results and questions. Never money to buy a position or for an offer abroad: it is corruption or a scam, and it always has a price. When the offer arrives, ask for it in writing, read the contract, never sign with blanks, check the duration, salary, trial period, notice period, and social security registration. If you have no job, don’t let it define you: follow a 90-day plan, earn a little money honestly while searching, control your spending, avoid debt, and don’t carry this alone. And always keep savings, a skill that sells, and a network: a job gets lost, a skill remains.

titre: M14.1 — Wealth creation: foundations and first income
objectifs: ✦  You know that all honest work produces abundance and that wealth begins where you are, with what you have.
✦  You know that succeeding means first of all living with purpose, and that wealth is its fruit, not its goal.
✦  You have written your map (dream, vision, mission, plan, values) and a one-page project.
✦  You know what a leader is, what keeps a leader standing, and what destroys one.
✦  You know the five phases of a project and you know how to build a solid business idea: market, model, financing, status.
✦  You know how to look for and secure a job without ever paying to be hired.

qcm.q: What does the sentence in Proverbs 14:23 say brings abundance?
c: Only prestigious work
Only well-paid work
All hard work
Big speeches and beautiful projects
qcm.e: The verse says neither “all prestigious work” nor “all well-paid work.” It says: all hard work. God put abundance in work, not in idle talk.

qcm.q: According to the introduction, where does wealth begin?
c: Where one has had a lot of schooling
Where one has inherited from a rich father
Where one holds a big position
Where you are, with what you have
qcm.e: Wealth does not begin at one particular place. You can start as a janitor or as a manager: the road is the same, work faithfully, learn, set aside, then make it bear fruit.

qcm.q: What does “financial freedom” mean in this module?
c: Becoming a billionaire
Never working again
Having your essential needs covered without being at the mercy of a single boss, a single salary, or a single creditor
No longer having to save
qcm.e: Savings for the bad days, no choking debts, several sources of income, and the ability to choose what you do with your days. It is not an end in itself: it allows you to serve more widely.

qcm.q: What does the introduction say about honest work?
c: It is slow, but shortcuts work better
It is the only solid road: shortcuts, bribes, and scams promise abundance and deliver poverty
It is only useful for getting started
It is only necessary for people without a diploma
qcm.e: What is acquired dishonestly does not last. Honest work is the only solid road.

qcm.q: According to the first key, what does it mean to succeed in life?
c: Getting rich as fast as possible
Finding meaning in your life and managing to live without regret; wealth can be its fruit, but it is not success itself
Having a diploma and a good position
Avoiding all failures
qcm.e: “Succeeding means, above all, managing to live.” You can make mistakes and suffer setbacks without having regret.

qcm.q: What is the “perilous block” described in the module?
c: Lack of diplomas
Lack of connections
Focusing on the money that is missing and giving up the project before even starting it
Having too many ideas at the same time
qcm.e: You will probably never have in hand all the money needed to start. Many things can be done without a penny: training, writing your project, observing your environment, testing.

qcm.q: What is a leader, according to the module?
c: The one who holds the highest position
The one who signs at the bottom of the page
The one who speaks best in public
The one who puts his influence at the service of those he leads, to guide them and help them grow
qcm.e: We confuse leadership with the position one holds. Jesus: “It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant.”

qcm.q: Among the four things that destroy a leader, which one opens the door to the others?
c: Pride
Manipulation
Emotional instability
Betrayal of one’s own values
qcm.e: Pride, manipulation, emotional instability, and the betrayal of one’s values almost never come together: pride opens the door, and the others walk in behind it. Saul serves as our warning.

qcm.q: Which of these statements is a SMART objective?
c: Helping young people
Training ten young girls in sewing in six months
Making the community grow
Succeeding with my sewing project
qcm.e: SMART: specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, and time-bound. “Helping young people” is not an objective.

qcm.q: What is the SWOT (FFOM) tool for?
c: Reviewing external factors: political, economic, social…
Calculating the price of a product
Taking stock of yourself: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats
Choosing the legal status
qcm.e: It is PESTEL that reviews what can affect you from the outside. SWOT takes stock of you and your situation.

qcm.q: What is the difference between a sole proprietorship and a SARL?
c: None, it is the same thing
In a sole proprietorship, your personal belongings answer for your debts; in a SARL, you risk only the amount of your contributions
A SARL is forbidden to a single person
In a SARL, the house can be affected, not in a sole proprietorship
qcm.e: If a sole proprietorship collapses, the house can be affected. A SARL can have just one person.

qcm.q: In Benin, at what annual turnover do you move from the TPS to the real tax regime?
c: 10 million F CFA
25 million F CFA
100 million F CFA
50 million F CFA
qcm.e: The TPS applies to small businesses whose annual turnover is below 50 million F CFA. Above that: the real tax regime, with VAT and tax on profits.

qcm.q: What does the Beninese paradox between a very low official unemployment and a very high underemployment show?
c: That almost no one has difficulty finding work
That the informal sector is a solution for everyone
That almost everyone has an activity, but many do not earn enough or not regularly: having a job is not always having a stable income
That diplomas are no longer of any use
qcm.e: The goal is not only to find a job, but a reasonably regular income with a minimum of security, and to keep it.

qcm.q: Someone offers, for 250,000 F, to get you into a government office without an exam. What do you do?
c: I accept: everybody does it
I refuse: it is corruption, and whoever gives in to get in ends up accepting other arrangements
I accept if I can pay in installments
I negotiate the price
qcm.e: “You shall take no bribe” (Exodus 23:8). The official fees for a file or an exam, when they exist, are announced in the official notice and are paid through the channel indicated. The rest, you refuse.

qcm.q: You are offered a job and told the contract will come later. What do you do?
c: I start Monday: it is a proof of trust
I start, but I ask for the contract in six months
I sign a paper with blanks, which the employer will fill in
I ask for the offer and the contract in writing before starting, I read them, and I keep a signed copy
qcm.e: What is written protects you as much as your employer. Never sign a paper with blanks, or a paper you have not understood.

qcm.q: You have been looking for a job for a long time. What attitude does the module recommend?
c: Wait for the opportunity to come
Follow a 90-day plan: get my affairs in order (CV, ANPE, contacts), search and learn with a weekly rhythm, then take stock; earn a little money honestly in the meantime
Hide my situation so as not to feel ashamed
Borrow to hold out during the search
qcm.e: The two dangers are immobility and shame. The ANPE is a free public service, with offices in all twelve departments. Tell your family, your partner, your pastor about your situation.

qcm.q: What does an employer look for first in someone he hires?
c: A diploma and a long CV
Reliability, competence, and attitude
A recommendation from a close contact
Someone who agrees not to be paid at first
qcm.e: An employer hopes the person will bring in more than they cost. He looks at reliability (on time, truthful, finishes what he starts), competence, and attitude.

qcm.q: The offers ask for experience you don’t have. What does the module recommend?
c: Giving up the search
Lying a little on your CV
Manufacturing experience: an internship, volunteering, a small assignment
Waiting for an offer with no conditions to appear
qcm.e: Proof that you have done something is worth more than the claim that you are capable of it. And lying on a CV always ends up being found out.

qcm.q: Which of these signs should alert you in a job offer?
c: The offer comes from the company’s official website
You are asked to pay, by Mobile Money to a personal number, to have a file reviewed
You are asked for your CV and a short letter
The company invites you to an interview
qcm.e: Paying to take a test, to have a file reviewed, or to “guarantee” a position or a visa is a sign of a scam or of corruption. Always verify with the institution itself.

qcm.q: In the 90-day plan, what do you do during days 1 to 30?
c: Take stock and change the angle of the search
Get my affairs in order: CV ready, ANPE registration, ten people informed, essential expenses noted
Wait for replies to applications
Create a business right away
qcm.e: Days 1 to 30 are for getting your affairs in order. Days 31 to 60, for searching and learning. Days 61 to 90, for taking stock and adjusting.
